narrative.note: Jordan, every single subject in this report is marked growing right now, and I want you to hear what that really means: Riley is four, and you're seeing him clearly at exactly the moment he is. This isn't a picture that needs fixing, it's a picture full of starting lines, all in one honest place. Since reading is what you asked about, that's exactly where I'd point first this month. Letter hunts and name tracing are small, low-pressure ways to build toward it, and there's no rush.

subjects.math: You haven't yet seen Riley count five objects one at a time and say how many, and that's a fine place to start. Counting stairs, crackers, or toy cars together, touching each one as he counts, builds this naturally.
subjects.literacy: Recognizing the letters in his own name is the next thing to watch for, and a daily letter hunt through cereal boxes and signs turns it into a game rather than a lesson.
subjects.phonics: Clapping the beats in a word, like ba-na-na, is the next step here, and sound-based I-spy is an easy way to practice it anywhere, even the car.
subjects.writing: Holding a crayon with fingers instead of a fist is the next thing to look for, and a big rainbow name he traces and decorates makes that grip practice feel like art time.
subjects.language: You haven't seen Riley narrate something that happened earlier in the day yet, and handing him the story after something fun, like telling dad about the park, gives him easy practice.
subjects.science: Sorting things into groups, big versus small, animals versus plants, is the next step, and a simple sink-or-float guessing game with five small objects makes that sorting hands-on.
subjects.social_studies: Naming family members and how they connect is the next thing to watch for, and drawing a map of your home together with a star on everyone's bed is a fun, low-key way in.
subjects.art: Naming main colors while drawing or painting is the next step, and putting on a song and drawing how it feels gives him a reason to reach for color words.
subjects.music: Clapping or tapping along to a steady beat is the next thing to watch for, and a simple copy-my-clap game, trading who leads, builds that rhythm sense.
subjects.gross_motor: Galloping with one foot leading is the next step, and animal races down the hallway, bear crawl to crab walk to frog jump, make big-body practice feel like play.
subjects.fine_motor: Stringing large beads or threading laces is the next thing to watch for, and snipping paper strips into confetti with child-safe scissors builds the same hand control.
subjects.social_emotional: Playing with other kids, taking turns and sharing with reminders, is the next step, and naming big feelings before offering two choices helps that turn-taking go smoother.
subjects.self_care: Daytime toilet use with only occasional misses is the next thing to watch for, and turning an old shirt into a button board makes related fine motor practice feel like a game, not a fight.
subjects.executive_function: Waiting a short turn without falling apart, with support, is the next step, and freeze dance is a fun, low-pressure way to practice that pause.
subjects.computer_science: This one is all about exposure, not age norms, and playing robot, where Riley gives you exact steps to follow, is a fun, screen-free way to introduce sequencing whenever you like.
subjects.spanish: This is exposure-based too, so there's no clock on it. Picking one useful phrase and using it all week at natural moments is a simple way to start.

narrative.synthesis: Every subject here reads as growing right now, and rather than sixteen separate to-dos, think of it as one four-year-old moving through a very normal, very full season all at once. Language, phonics, and letter recognition are really one pre-reading story, so a bit of daily narrating, sound play, and letter hunting all feed the same goal you named: reading. Fine motor pieces, crayon grip and snipping, quietly support writing too. Given that Riley loves trucks, you could fold that in almost anywhere: count the trucks on the stairs, sort big trucks from small ones, or have him narrate a truck adventure back to you. If you want one place to put your energy this month, I'd start with letters and sounds together, since that's the thread that leads most directly toward reading, and everything else can follow at its own pace.

drawers.math: Riley hasn't yet counted five objects one at a time while saying how many there are, which is a skill that typically shows up by four. Counting real things around the house, touching each one as he goes, gives him repeated, low-pressure practice building toward it.
drawers.literacy: Recognizing the letters in his own name usually shows up by three and a half, so this is a clear next target. A daily letter hunt, picking one letter and spotting it everywhere, builds recognition through play instead of drills.
drawers.phonics: Clapping the beats in a word is a skill that typically appears by four, and it's not yet something you've seen from Riley. Playing I-spy with sounds instead of objects gives him easy, everyday reps.
drawers.writing: Holding a crayon with fingers rather than a fist typically develops by four, and Riley isn't there yet. Tracing his name in different colors builds that grip strength while feeling like a fun art project.
drawers.language: Telling you about something that happened earlier in the day typically emerges by four, and this hasn't shown up yet for Riley. Prompting him to retell a fun moment to another person gives him low-stakes narrating practice.
drawers.science: Sorting things into groups, like big versus small, typically develops by three and a half. A hands-on guessing game, like sink or float, turns that sorting skill into something playful rather than academic.
drawers.social_studies: Naming family members and how they connect typically shows up by just under four, and it's the next thing to watch for with Riley. Drawing a simple map of home together introduces this concept concretely.
drawers.art: Naming main colors while creating typically appears by three and a half. Drawing along to music gives him a natural reason to reach for and use color words.
drawers.music: Clapping or tapping to a steady beat is a skill that typically shows by around this age, and it's the next one to watch for. A simple echo-clap game builds that rhythm sense through back-and-forth play.
drawers.gross_motor: Galloping with one foot leading typically develops by four. Animal-themed races give him varied, playful practice with big-body coordination.
drawers.fine_motor: Stringing large beads or threading laces typically shows up around this age. Snipping paper into strips builds the same hand strength and control in a lower-pressure way.
drawers.social_emotional: Playing with other kids, including turn-taking and sharing with reminders, typically develops around this age. Naming feelings before offering choices helps him practice the self-regulation that turn-taking requires.
drawers.self_care: Daytime toilet independence, with only occasional misses, typically develops by four. A playful button board builds related fine motor skills while easing pressure around self-care routines.
drawers.executive_function: Waiting a short turn without falling apart, even with support, typically develops around this age. Freeze dance is a fun way to build that pause-and-control muscle.
drawers.computer_science: This is exposure-based, so there's no age benchmark to meet, just a fun step-by-step game, playing robot, that introduces sequencing whenever it fits your family's rhythm.
drawers.spanish: This is also exposure-based, with no timeline attached. Choosing one everyday phrase and using it consistently for a week is a simple, sustainable way to start.

narrative.keepsake: Riley, right now you are all about trucks, big ones, small ones, the ones that rumble down the street. You notice things and you want to talk about them, and that curiosity is going to take you so far. Your mom has watched you count things around the house, try out crayons and colors, and dance and clap along to music, just because it's fun. You're learning new words and new moves every single day, and you're doing it your own way, at your own pace. Keep looking closely at the world, Riley, it's a wonderful thing to watch. With love, Homa.
